claim: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is one of the major causes of morbidity and mortality in the Western World.
source: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is one of the major causes of morbidity and mortality in the Western World (Center for Disease Control, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Center for Disease Control, 2013

claim: Vulnerable plaques are atherosclerotic plaques that do not yet limit flow in the coronary artery but may potentially cause an acute coronary syndrome by rupturing with subsequent acute occlusion of the artery.
source: One of the main challenges in modern therapy of patients with CAD is the detection of atherosclerotic plaques that do not yet limit flow in the coronary artery, but may potentially cause an acute coronary syndrome by rupturing with subsequent acute occlusion of the artery. Decades ago, these lesion entities have been defined as 'vulnerable plaques' (Virmani et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Virmani et al., 2003

claim: Pathology-based studies have been used to explore potential features of plaque vulnerability.
source: Pathology-based studies (Virmani et al., 2003; Falk, 1989; Burke et al., 1997; Virmani et al., 2000) as well as intravascular imaging (Kato et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2013; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012; Ehara et al., 2004) have been used over time to explore potential features of plaque vulnerability, that is morphological characteristics which may predispose a plaque to rupture.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to pathology-based studies

claim: Intravascular imaging has been used to explore potential features of plaque vulnerability.
source: Pathology-based studies (Virmani et al., 2003; Falk, 1989; Burke et al., 1997; Virmani et al., 2000) as well as intravascular imaging (Kato et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2013; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012; Ehara et al., 2004) have been used over time to explore potential features of plaque vulnerability, that is morphological characteristics which may predispose a plaque to rupture.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to intravascular imaging studies

claim: Presently accepted features of plaque vulnerability assessed using intravascular imaging include the thickness of the fibrous cap.
source: The presently accepted features assessed using intravascular imaging include the thickness of the fibrous cap (FCT) (Kato et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2013; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012), the extent of the necrotic lipid core (Kato et al., 2012), the presence of macrophages (Kato et al., 2012; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012), microvessels (Kato et al., 2012; Uemura et al., 2012), small calcifications (Ehara et al., 2004; Reith et al., 2018), or a positive remodeling (Varnava et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on fibrous cap thickness

claim: Presently accepted features of plaque vulnerability assessed using intravascular imaging include the extent of the necrotic lipid core.
source: The presently accepted features assessed using intravascular imaging include the thickness of the fibrous cap (FCT) (Kato et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2013; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012), the extent of the necrotic lipid core (Kato et al., 2012), the presence of macrophages (Kato et al., 2012; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012), microvessels (Kato et al., 2012; Uemura et al., 2012), small calcifications (Ehara et al., 2004; Reith et al., 2018), or a positive remodeling (Varnava et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kato et al., 2012

claim: Features of coronary plaque vulnerability may be assessed with coronary computed tomography angiography and include low-attenuation plaques and a higher plaque burden.
source: Features of coronary plaque vulnerability may also be assessed with different imaging modalities, such as coronary computed tomography angiography, and include also low-attenuation plaques and a higher plaque burden (Conte et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conte et al., 2017

claim: High-risk plaque features may predict the incidence of future major cardiac events.
source: These features may predict the incidence of future major cardiac events (Conte et al., 2017; Prati et al., 2020), if such high-risk plaques are not timely recognized and sealed (Dettori et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Conte et al., 2017 and Prati et al., 2020

claim: Plaque rupture originates from an excessive stress concentration on the fibrous cap, which trespasses the tensile strength of the material and ultimately causes material failure.
source: From a mechanistic perspective, plaque rupture originates from an excessive stress concentration on the fibrous cap, which trespasses the tensile strength of the material and ultimately causes material failure and consequently plaque rupture.
evidence: Based on mechanistic reasoning about material failure

claim: The fibrous cap yields a protective effect by avoiding the exposure of prothrombotic material present in the necrotic lipid core.
source: The fibrous cap yields, in this view, a protective effect, by avoiding the exposure of prothrombotic material present in the necrotic lipid core.
evidence: Based on established understanding of fibrous cap function

claim: Minimal fibrous cap thickness has been considered the most established parameter of plaque vulnerability.
source: Thus, it is not surprising that minimal FCT has been considered the most established parameter of plaque vulnerability (Kato et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2013; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012): in fact, the thickness of the fibrous cap seems a good surrogate parameter of its ability to resist stresses.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on fibrous cap thickness

claim: The thickness of the fibrous cap seems a good surrogate parameter of its ability to resist stresses.
source: Thus, it is not surprising that minimal FCT has been considered the most established parameter of plaque vulnerability (Kato et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2013; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012): in fact, the thickness of the fibrous cap seems a good surrogate parameter of its ability to resist stresses.
evidence: Based on logical inference about material properties

claim: Evaluating solely the fibrous cap addresses only the main stabilizing factor in plaque biomechanics, leaving the destabilizing factors almost completely ignored.
source: Still, evaluating solely the fibrous cap addresses only the main stabilizing factor in plaque biomechanics, leaving the destabilizing factors almost completely ignored.
evidence: Based on logical analysis of current approaches

claim: Plaque rupture occurs if the stress within coronary lesions exceeds the protection exerted by the fibrous cap.
source: However, plaque rupture occurs if the stress within coronary lesions exceeds the protection exerted by the fibrous cap.
evidence: Based on mechanistic understanding of material failure

claim: Very little is known about the determinants of the disrupting force pushing coronary plaques to rupture.
source: However, very little is known about the determinants of the disrupting force pushing coronary plaques to rupture.
evidence: Assessment of current state of knowledge

claim: The spatial relationship between rupture and the balance of stabilizing and destabilizing forces in the plaque remains largely unexplored.
source: In addition, the spatial relationship between rupture and the balance of stabilizing and destabilizing forces in the plaque remains largely unexplored: in other words, whether plaque rupture occurs at the site with the lowest FCT, as point of least resistance, or rather in sites of highest stress concentration, as point of maximal disruption is unclear.
evidence: Assessment of current state of knowledge

claim: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is an established intravascular imaging technique with supreme resolution (up to 10–20 µm) that is able to depict peri-luminal structures with high accuracy.
source: As a source of patient-specific, high-quality images of coronary plaques for this proof-of-concept study, we selected optical coherence tomography (OCT), an established intravascular imaging technique which, due to a supreme resolution (up to 10–20 µm), is able to depict peri-luminal structures with high accuracy (Burgmaier et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burgmaier et al., 2014

claim: In ruptured lesions, maximal stress within fibrous cap (peak cap stress) was 174 ± 67 kPa compared to 52 ± 42 kPa in non-ruptured lesions (p<0.001).
source: In ruptured lesions, maximal stress within fibrous cap (peak cap stress [PCS]: 174 ± 67 vs. 52 ± 42 kPa, p<0.001) and vessel wall (maximal plaque stress [MPS]: 399 ± 233 vs. 90 ± 95 kPa, p=0.001) were significantly higher compared to non-ruptured plaques.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from finite-element analysis

claim: In ruptured lesions, maximal stress within vessel wall (maximal plaque stress) was 399 ± 233 kPa compared to 90 ± 95 kPa in non-ruptured lesions (p=0.001).
source: In ruptured lesions, maximal stress within fibrous cap (peak cap stress [PCS]: 174 ± 67 vs. 52 ± 42 kPa, p<0.001) and vessel wall (maximal plaque stress [MPS]: 399 ± 233 vs. 90 ± 95 kPa, p=0.001) were significantly higher compared to non-ruptured plaques.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from finite-element analysis

claim: Ruptures arose in the immediate proximity of maximal stress concentrations with angular distances of 21.8 ± 30.3° for peak cap stress and 20.7 ± 23.7° for maximal plaque stress.
source: Ruptures arose in the immediate proximity of maximal stress concentrations (angular distances: 21.8 ± 30.3° for PCS vs. 20.7 ± 23.7° for MPS); stress concentrations excellently predicted plaque rupture (area under the curve: 0.940 for PCS, 0.950 for MPS).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from spatial correlation analysis

claim: Stress concentrations excellently predicted plaque rupture with area under the curve of 0.940 for peak cap stress and 0.950 for maximal plaque stress.
source: Ruptures arose in the immediate proximity of maximal stress concentrations (angular distances: 21.8 ± 30.3° for PCS vs. 20.7 ± 23.7° for MPS); stress concentrations excellently predicted plaque rupture (area under the curve: 0.940 for PCS, 0.950 for MPS).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ROC analysis

claim: The prediction of plaque rupture by stress concentrations was superior to established vulnerability features such as fibrous cap thickness or macrophage infiltration.
source: This prediction of plaque rupture was superior to established vulnerability features such as fibrous cap thickness or macrophage infiltration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing ROC curves

claim: OCT-based finite-element analysis effectively assesses plaque biomechanics, which in turn predicts plaque rupture in patients.
source: In conclusion, OCT-based finite-element analysis effectively assesses plaque biomechanics, which in turn predicts plaque rupture in patients.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: Twenty patients with type 2 diabetes were enrolled in this study.
source: Of the 20 patients with type 2 diabetes enrolled in this study, 10 underwent coronary angiography due to acute coronary syndrome and 10 due to chronic coronary syndrome.
evidence: Supported by study design data

source: Of the 20 patients with type 2 diabetes enrolled in this study, 10 underwent coronary angiography due to acute coronary syndrome and 10 due to chronic coronary syndrome.

source: Patients with (n = 10) and without (n = 10) plaque rupture did not differ with respect to their clinical characteristics, apart from a worse glycemic control in patients with plaque rupture (HbA1c: 7.4 ± 1.4 vs. 6.1 ± 0.5, p=0.026).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from patient characteristics

claim: Ruptured lesions presented a lower minimal fibrous cap thickness (49 ± 10 µm vs. 97 ± 15 µm, p<0.001) compared to non-ruptured lesions.
source: As expected, ruptured lesions presented a lower FCT (minimal FCT: 49 ± 10 µm vs. 97 ± 15 µm, p<0.001; mean FCT: 94 ± 17 µm vs. 133 ± 12 µm, p=0.006), a more extensive necrotic lipid core (lipid arc: 178 ± 39° vs. 110 ± 8°, p=0.001; lipid volume index: 9876 ± 3088 vs. 3853 ± 1294, p=0.011), and a higher incidence of thin-capped fibroatheromas (70% vs. 0%, p=0.003) compared to non-ruptured lesions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from OCT analysis

source: Optimal cut-off for prediction of plaque rupture were 150.5 kPa (Sensitivity 90%; Specificity 80%) for peak cap stress and 169.5 kPa (Sensitivity 90%; Specificity 90%) for maximal plaque stress.

claim: The optimal cut-off for prediction of plaque rupture was 169.5 kPa (Sensitivity 90%; Specificity 90%) for maximal plaque stress.

claim: The CLIMA score could predict plaque rupture with an area under the curve of 0.870.
source: Both scores could predict plaque rupture with very good to excellent diagnostic efficiency (AUC for CLIMA score: 0.870; AUC for Burgmaier score: 0.900), which however remained numerically lower than results of our morpho-mechanic analysis.

claim: Higher stress concentrations both within the fibrous cap and within the whole plaque in ruptured plaques compared to non-ruptured plaques is in line with previous simulation studies based on pathology specimens.
source: First, we could in vivo detect higher stress concentrations both within the fibrous cap and within the whole plaque in ruptured plaques compared to non-ruptured plaques. This is in line with previous simulation studies based on pathology specimens (Loree et al., 1992; Cheng et al., 1993) and confirms our hypothesis of stress concentration as a central factor in the genesis of plaque rupture.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The spatial coincidence between maximal stress concentrations and sites of plaque rupture confirms the causal link between plaque biomechanics and plaque rupture.
source: This spatial coincidence between maximal stress concentrations and sites of plaque rupture confirms the causal link between plaque biomechanics on the one hand and plaque rupture and acute coronary syndromes on the other.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data on spatial correlation

claim: Stress within the fibrous cap and overall within the plaque is concentrated in a pattern which is closely dependent on the morphology of the plaque.
source: Stress within the fibrous cap and overall within the plaque is concentrated in a pattern which is closely dependent on the morphology of the plaque (for instance, in dependence of the extent and morphology of the necrotic lipid core and/or of calcification).
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data and mechanistic understanding

claim: Material failure and plaque rupture occurs when stress concentration trespasses the ultimate tensile strength of the vessel wall, which is highly likely to happen in points of maximal stress concentration.
source: A specific force is exerted on each point of the fibrous cap; should this stress concentration trespass the ultimate tensile strength of the vessel wall – which is highly likely to happen in points of maximal stress concentration – material failure and, eventually, plaque rupture occurs.
evidence: Based on mechanistic reasoning about material failure

claim: A previous pathology-based study by Cheng et al., 1993 sets the stress threshold for plaque rupture to 300 kPa.
source: A previous pathology-based study by Cheng et al., 1993 sets the stress threshold for plaque rupture to 300 kPa.

claim: In pathology specimens, the fixation process may cause a shrinkage of the fibrous cap with a shortening of ca. 10–20% compared to the thickness measured in vivo with OCT.
source: In fact, in pathology specimens (on which the 300 kPa value is based on), the fixation process may cause a shrinkage of the fibrous cap with a shortening of ca. 10–20% compared to the thickness measured in vivo with OCT.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about tissue fixation effects

claim: The relationship between fibrous cap thickness and peak cap stress is exponential.
source: This effect may be sufficient to explain the numerical difference of the 'critical' peak cap stress needed for plaque rupture, especially considering – as pointed out by Finet et al. – that the relationship between FCT and peak cap stress is exponential (Finet et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Finet et al., 2004

claim: Hyperelastic behavior of certain plaque components has been described by some authors previously.

claim: The diagnostic efficiency of the finite-element analysis model was clearly superior compared with accepted parameters of plaque vulnerability such as fibrous cap thickness or plaque macrophage infiltration.
source: Furthermore, the model we developed presented a clearly superior diagnostic efficiency compared with accepted parameters of plaque vulnerability as FCT (Kato et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2013; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012) or plaque macrophage infiltration (Kato et al., 2012; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012) and a numerically superior efficiency when compared to lipid volume index (Kato et al., 2012) in our cohort.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ROC comparison

claim: The diagnostic efficiency of the finite-element analysis model was numerically superior when compared to lipid volume index.
source: Furthermore, the model we developed presented a clearly superior diagnostic efficiency compared with accepted parameters of plaque vulnerability as FCT (Kato et al., 2012; Kubo et al., 2013; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012) or plaque macrophage infiltration (Kato et al., 2012; Reith et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2012) and a numerically superior efficiency when compared to lipid volume index (Kato et al., 2012) in our cohort.

claim: The diagnostic efficiency of the finite-element analysis model was comparable to the combination of lesion morphologies including fibrous cap thickness, plaque macrophage infiltration, and lipid volume index.

claim: This study is the first to develop an OCT-based finite-element model allowing patient-specific analysis of plaque biomechanics.
source: To the best of our knowledge, although we are first to develop an OCT-based finite-element model allowing patient-specific analysis of plaque biomechanics, several limitations have to be acknowledged.
evidence: Authors' assessment of novelty of their work

claim: The study faithfully reproduced plaque morphology in a 2D-based reconstruction.
source: First of all, we faithfully reproduced plaque morphology in a 2D-based reconstruction; on the other hand, we are not taking into account several phenomena that may influence stress concentration, as for instance the longitudinal structure of the plaque or the longitudinal profile of the stenosis and flow shear stress – the relevance of these factors needs to be addressed in future studies.
evidence: Description of study methodology

claim: The study did not take into account the longitudinal structure of the plaque or the longitudinal profile of the stenosis and flow shear stress.

claim: Limited light penetration of OCT to the deeper vessel wall may cause imprecisions in the segmentation.
source: Furthermore, in spite of the excellent resolution of OCT in the near field, we cannot exclude imprecisions in the segmentation due to limited light penetration to the deeper vessel wall.

claim: Limited tissue penetration of OCT does not allow to assess sites with positive remodeling.
source: Limited tissue penetration, in fact, does not allow to assess sites with positive remodeling, which may yield higher stresses due to accelerated plaque growth and therefore cause a higher rupture risk.
evidence: Based on known limitations of OCT technology

claim: Sites with positive remodeling may yield higher stresses due to accelerated plaque growth and therefore cause a higher rupture risk.
source: Limited tissue penetration, in fact, does not allow to assess sites with positive remodeling, which may yield higher stresses due to accelerated plaque growth and therefore cause a higher rupture risk.

claim: The study employed a linear elastic model for finite-element analysis.
source: For our study, we employed a linear elastic model; other authors, though, suggest an hyperelastic behavior of the vessel wall, particularly for displacements > 20% of the initial dimensions (Yang et al., 2009; Kobielarz et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of study methodology

claim: The average displacement in the study was 10%.
source: In spite of an average displacement 'small enough' (10%) to justify linearity, we cannot exclude underestimation of stress concentrations for very few plaques with larger displacements.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from finite-element analysis

claim: This study is the first to employ a morpho-metric approach in assessing plaque vulnerability on in vivo intravascular imaging.
source: To the best of our knowledge, although being the first to employ a morpho-metric approach in assessing plaque vulnerability on in vivo intravascular imaging, this pilot study still includes a low number of patients chosen among patients with and without plaque rupture, which may reduce the reliability of exact AUC and cut-off values in our predictive models; further analyses are needed to confirm the results of our proof-of-concept analysis.
evidence: Authors' assessment of novelty of their work

claim: The pilot study includes a low number of patients which may reduce the reliability of exact AUC and cut-off values in the predictive models.
